extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, law students, and inventors drafting or litigating patent specifications
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for drafting and construing patent specifications: what must be disclosed, how broadly a principle may be claimed, and the enablement and honesty duties owed to the public. Intended to guide patentees and courts in evaluating sufficiency and scope of specifications and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: No patent for an abstract principle; must claim a practical mode
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential that the specification should describe some practical mode of carrying the principle into effect; the patentable subject-matter is the mode of carrying the principle into effect, not the principle itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim merely stating cutting ice by any non-human power was void. The specification must describe a practical mode so that the claim is for the mode, not the abstract principle. If only a principle is appropriated, the claim is void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe at least one embodiment/machinery to show application
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee is bound to describe some machinery or practical method of making the application in order to show that he has actually applied the principle and to enable others to do so after him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The means by which the patentee has made the application must be described; omission to show an embodiment that applies the principle is fatal. Neilson and Watt examples: Watt carried his condensation principle into effect by describing a mode—this supported the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of means that produces same effect can infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: A variation of the means and machinery, if it produces the same beneficial effect (i.e., is the same application of the same principle), does not show non-infringement and may still infringe the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the patentee described a particular form, other shapes/implementations that apply the same principle to produce the same effect may be within the patentee's rights (see Minter's self-adjusting chair).

rubrics_metrics.name: May claim the mode of applying a principle generally (not confined to one form)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor suggests and invents how the principle may be applied to a practical result by mechanical contrivance, and shows that no particular sort or modification of apparatus is essential, he may claim the mode of carrying the principle into effect without confining to one form of apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neilson's hot-blast patent allowed claim to heating the blast in any vessel shape because the patentee showed the application and indicated shape was 'immaterial to the effect.' General claims covering all apparatus that effect the stated object can be sustained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality of claim (all modes) is not per se objectionable
rubrics_metrics.description: A general claim that includes every mode of applying the principle to produce a specified result is not an objection in law; the comprehensiveness is often the merit of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Justice Clerk Hope's directions: including many modes, even if some are better than others, only shows the invention's beauty and utility; it does not invalidate the patent if a practicable mode is disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: When claiming a combination, every claimed component must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification describes several things, and one or more of them is not new, the court must decide whether the patent can be sustained as a patent for the combination; a patent for a combination of three things cannot at the same time be a patent for any two of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General principle: combination claims are for the whole combination as claimed; you cannot simultaneously claim all subcombinations as the same invention. Courts examine novelty of each component when construing combination claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of honesty — no concealment or fraudulent additions
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must not mislead the public by concealing anything material to the invention or by adding anything not necessary to produce the described effect for the purpose of deceiving the public; the statute makes this a defence to an action on a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fraudulent concealment of material facts or addition of useless/non-necessary matter known to be so at preparation time will defeat the patent. If something later proves useless, patent is not affected; the focus is on intent at drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement: full, clear, and exact description to enable skilled persons
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute requires the patentee to describe the manner and process of making, constructing, using, and compounding his invention in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity, as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it appertains to make, construct, compound, and use the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core enablement requirement; failure to meet it is a factual question for the jury. The specification must enable without undue experimentation and must particularly point out the part or combination claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: For machines: explain the principle and several contemplated modes; particularly specify claimed part/improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: In case of any machine, the patentee shall fully explain the principle and the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his own invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification should both teach the inventive principle and illustrate multiple modes/applications where relevant, and must clearly identify what is claimed so the public understands the monopoly's scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement standard: persons of reasonably competent skill (not highest experts or laymen)
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must enable 'persons of competent skill' in the art — practical workmen or persons of reasonably competent skill — not those possessing the highest degree of skill, nor ordinary day-laborers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification need not teach to the level of top experts, but must be sufficient that a person of ordinary competent skill can reproduce the invention without inventing new features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable reproduction without invention or additions
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must enable persons of competent skill and knowledge to construct or reproduce the thing described without invention or addition of their own and without repeated experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is insufficient if the specification leaves material details to be supplied by the workman or sets a problem that requires inventive effort to solve (Morgan v. Seaward). A competent workman should be able to carry it out by applying ordinary trade knowledge only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require undue experiments or seeing others make it
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification is insufficient if information must be derived from experiments or from seeing others make the thing described; it must enable construction from the specification alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliance on subsequent experimental correction or on observing the defendant's implementation is not allowed to save a deficient specification (Neilson v. Harford).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose material parameters (materials, form, speed, relative dimensions) when they are material
rubrics_metrics.description: Any material alteration to be made in existing apparatus must be stated and not left to be supplied by the workman — e.g., materials employed, their form, the speed of parts, or their relative dimensions where these are material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such material parameters are omitted and are necessary to make the invention work, the specification will be insufficient because it forces the skilled person to invent or experiment to supply them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slight defects that require inventive power render the specification (and patent) invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: Slight defects in a specification that create a necessity for the exercise of inventive power on the part of the person undertaking to apply it will render the patent void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If competent persons would have to 'set themselves a problem to solve' or exercise invention to make the patent work, the specification is inadequate and the patent fails (instruction to jury standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of matter affecting only degree of benefit is not fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: The omission to mention something which contributes only to the degree of benefit, provided the apparatus would work beneficially and be worth adopting, is not necessarily a fatal defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between omissions essential to achieve the invention's purpose (fatal) and omissions that only tune or increase the degree of benefit (not fatal). Courts assess whether the disclosed mode produces some useful and beneficial result.
